ev.intro: A warning is only useful if acting on it costs less than the damage it prevents. That trade is different for everyone, so pick yours:

ev.scale: A perfect forecast is <0>100%</0>. Never looking at the forecast at all — always act, or never act — is <0>0%</0>.
ev.atPeak: This is the trade where the model helps most.
ev.peak: It helps most at <0>₹{{r}}</0>, where it reaches <1>{{pct}}%</1>.
ev.axes: Left to right: what acting costs you, in rupees per ₹100 of damage. Up the side: how much of a perfect forecast's value you keep. The curve peaks in the middle because that is where a warning actually changes what you would have done anyway.

mp.serverNote: The serving copy carries the cycles needed to score today and to replay recent ones — not the full training archive, which lives where the model is trained. Region ids count every id it holds: the 666 districts, plus one point per state or UT from cycles scored before the live feed moved to districts on 23 Sep.
mp.serverSince: The model itself was trained on data going back to <0>{{y}}</0>; this range is only what this 512 MB box carries.
mp.bustBody: A forecast busts when its error exceeds this variable's own threshold, the <0>{{pct}}</0> percentile of its error on the training data. <0>Bust above</0> is taken over the ensemble average's error per district and day, which is what a bust is judged on. <0>p90 error</0> is the same percentile for a single member's forecast, used only to scale the confidence figures. One member misses by more than the ensemble average does, so it is the larger.
mp.anyVar: A district-day is a bust if any one of its {{k}} variables busts, and each does on {{each}}% of training forecasts by construction. Were the {{k}} independent, {{indep}}% of district-days would bust; they move together, and on the held-out year <0>{{actual}}%</0> did.
mp.flagged: A region is flagged <0>watch</0> above <1>{{w}}%</1> and <0>bust</0> above <1>{{b}}%</1>.
mp.errTitle: Error per variable, against a baseline that always predicts the average error
mp.errNote: The baseline predicts the same error for every forecast - the average over the rows being scored - so it cannot tell one forecast from another. Skill = 1 − MAE ÷ baseline MAE: the share of its error the model removes. Positive is better than the baseline. MAE is the average miss, RMSE the same thing but weighted towards the big misses, and R² the share of the variation the model accounts for.
mp.ladderNote: Each baseline is fitted on the training split alone and scored on the same held-out rows as the classifier. Skill vs climatology is 0.000 for simply guessing the long-run bust rate every time; higher is better.
mp.arrows: ↓ lower is better · ↑ higher is better
ab.title: What this is
ab.sub: Sanket — संकेत, “signal”. Predicting where a weather forecast will be wrong, and saying why.
ab.start: <0>Start here:</0> Replay takes a real forecast cycle from the archive, scores it with the deployed model, and shows what this system would have told a forecaster that day — before anyone knew the outcome.
ab.q1: Every operational centre already issues a forecast. This does not try to make a better one. It answers the question a duty forecaster actually has at 6am:
ab.q2: “How likely is the forecast I am holding to be badly wrong today?”
ab.q3: Correction and confidence are different services. NCMRWF already corrects its forecasts statistically, and busts still happen. Correction removes the errors a model makes <0>consistently</0>; a bust comes from the particular weather pattern of that day, which is not consistent and so is not corrected away. Knowing when to distrust a forecast is what decides whether a warning goes out.
ab.q4: A <0>bust</0> is a forecast whose error lands in the tail of that variable’s own historical error distribution — the 90th percentile, computed on training data only. Each variable therefore has its own threshold, in its own units:
ab.reading: <0>Reading these:</0> ROC-AUC is the chance the model ranks a real bust above a non-bust — 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. F1 balances how often its warnings are right against how many busts it catches. Brier is the average error in the probability itself, so lower is better.
ab.measured: Measured on the <0>{{split}}</0> split — forecast cycles the model never trained on
ab.caution: One caution, found in our own data and being fixed rather than hidden: for temperature, humidity and soil moisture most large errors are the same districts being off in the same direction every day — a steady bias that ordinary bias correction already removes — rather than a forecast failing on a particular day. The next model defines a bust on bias-corrected error, so a warning means “today is unusual”, not “this district is always off”.
ab.cmp: Every baseline is fitted on the training split alone and scored on the same held-out rows as the model. Each is compared against climatology — simply guessing the long-run bust rate every time. <0>0.000 means it does no better than that guess</0>; higher is better.
ab.leadCorr: Guessing from the lead day alone scores about zero skill, because busts do not simply become more likely further out. The measured link between lead day and bust is only {{train}} on training data and {{test}} on held-out data.
ab.noLadder: The baseline comparison is generated by the training run; this model predates it and the table is written on the next retrain.
ab.svcTitle: Use it as a service, not just a page
ab.svc: Every number on this site is read from a public, documented HTTP API — the same one this page calls. There is no private back channel and no figure baked into the frontend. <0>17 endpoints</0>, schema-checked with Pydantic and described by an auto-generated OpenAPI document, so a forecast desk could pull bust risk straight into its own tooling.
ab.docs: <0>Interactive docs</0> — <1>/docs</1> (Swagger UI, every endpoint callable from the browser — start here), and the raw schema at <2>/openapi.json</2> (machine-readable, for code generators — it opens as one long line of JSON).
ab.endpoints: <0>The ones worth starting with</0> (these return raw JSON for software, not a readable page) — <1>/api/regions/all</1> for every district at every lead day, <2>/api/alerts</2> for what is above the watch level right now, and <3>/api/model/status</3> for the scores on this page, straight from the served model.
ab.fair: <0>Fair warning</0> — this is a free-tier box that sleeps after 15 minutes idle, so a first call can take 30–50 seconds to wake it. That is the cost of the $0 hosting, not a fault.
ab.trustTitle: Why the numbers can be trusted
ab.t1: <0>No synthetic, mocked or placeholder data anywhere</0> — not even as a fallback. Where a number cannot be computed from real data, this interface shows an em dash <1>and the reason</1>. That rule is enforced in the code, not just stated here.
ab.t2: <0>Real data end to end.</0> NOAA’s GEFS forecasts — historical re-runs for training, the live feed for today — checked against ERA5, a reconstructed record of what the weather actually did.
ab.t3: <0>Leakage is tested for, and a leak we found is written down.</0> Bust thresholds are fitted on the training split only; whole forecast runs are kept together so the model is never tested on a run it partly trained on; and no observed day appears on both sides of the train/test split — each a test in the suite. A later audit still found one input that looked at an observation from after the forecast was issued; it is documented in the project’s known issues and removed in the next retrain, and scores are re-measured then.
ab.t4: <0>Even the “truth” we score against is uncertain.</0> Two leading global weather records disagree with each other by roughly a quarter to a half of a bust threshold, measured over ~21,000 city-days. Stated up front rather than waiting to be asked.
ab.n1: <0>A re-run archive, not the live model’s own history.</0> The model learns from NOAA’s reforecast — the forecast model re-run once a day for past years with 5 ensemble members — and some variables stop early there: 10 m wind at Day 5, soil moisture at Day 3. Those are not scored beyond that, even though the live feed carries all ten days.
ab.n2: <0>One geography now, not two.</0> The live feed used to sample the nearest grid point at 36 station locations, one per state and union territory, while the training archive covered all 666 districts as an area-weighted mean of every 0.25° cell each polygon overlaps. Since 2026-09-23 the live feed uses the same area-weighted method over the same 666 districts, so a live cycle and the archive behind the model describe geography the same way.
ab.n3: GEFS runs 31 parallel forecasts; this uses 5 of them. How much those disagree is one of the model’s inputs, so that input is noisier here than it would be with all 31.
ab.n4: ERA5 precipitation is weak over India relative to gauge-based products, and rainfall results carry that caveat. Rainfall is also the hardest variable here: most days have none at all, and the rest are dominated by a few extreme ones.
ab.n5: <0>It does not send alerts to anyone.</0> Warnings appear in this interface and nowhere else — there is no SMS, email or push delivery, and nothing is dispatched to a duty desk. This is a decision-support view a forecaster reads, not a warning system that acts on its own.
ab.n6: A bust is defined on <0>surface-variable error</0>, not the synoptic Z500 criterion of Rodwell et al. (2013). That is a deliberate choice: surface error is what reaches agriculture and disaster response, whereas Z500 is what reaches meteorologists.
ab.runs: FastAPI and XGBoost behind React and TypeScript, over a hive-partitioned Parquet store — one origin, one process. Training runs on CI with 16 GB; the site is served from a 512 MB free-tier instance that <0>cannot train</0>, which is why serving memory was cut to fit with scored output verified byte-identical at every step. When the upstream feed drops forecast steps mid-pull, a fallback source refills them before the daily reduction — a short rainfall <1>sum</1> would otherwise silently halve the quantity that drives most busts. Total hosting cost: nothing.
ab.d1: <0>Forecasts</0> — NOAA GEFSv12, the reforecast archive (2000–2019, one 00 UTC cycle a day, 5 ensemble members) for training, the live operational feed for today. Public domain, via NOAA's Open Data bucket on AWS S3.
ab.d2: <0>Observations</0> — ERA5 reanalysis from the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), licensed CC-BY 4.0: from the Climate Data Store for training, and via the Open-Meteo Historical Weather API for recent days (<1>Weather data by Open-Meteo.com</1>). Contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information 2026. Some training years also carry IMD–NCMRWF merged satellite-gauge rainfall (India Meteorological Department).
ab.d3: <0>Other inputs</0> — the MJO index is NOAA PSL’s OLR-based MJO Index (OMI); district elevation is CGIAR-CSI SRTM 250 m from the International Centre for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), via the Open-Elevation API.
ab.d4: <0>District boundaries</0> — GADM 4.1, India admin-2 (gadm.org). Two corrections are applied before use: Ladakh is reassigned out of Jammu & Kashmir, since GADM predates the 2019 reorganisation; and disputed-territory features are kept and dissolved into their parent district rather than filtered out, so Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh still appear on the map. Used here for a non-commercial hackathon prototype — formal licence review for any use beyond that is not yet done.
ab.d5: <0>Open-source software</0> — Sanket's code is MIT-licensed. The libraries in this page are listed with their licences in <1>third-party-licenses.txt</1>; every other dependency, dataset and font is in the repository's <2>third-party notices</2>.
ab.d6: <0>The project.</0> Built for Smart India Hackathon 2026, Problem Statement 26079, set by the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
